text: Let's call it what it is: what happened between Miss Mexico and Nawat wasn’t some grand moral fight. It was a trivial procedural disagreement that exploded only because it was handled without emotional intelligence. A Miss Universe candidate is expected to carry herself like an ambassador, not like someone itching for a public showdown over a social-media post. Even if Nawat’s tone was out of line, the sashing event—filled with delegates who simply wanted to continue and enjoy the evening—was absolutely the worst place to escalate. One calm line—“I’ll discuss this with my team and get back to you”—would have ended the tension immediately. That’s basic professionalism. That’s what adults do in any serious workplace when a cross-department conflict arises. What made the entire thing even more disappointing was the attempt to cloak a minor logistical misunderstanding in grand slogans like “my voice should be heard” and “this is women’s empowerment.” Put it plainly: misusing these phrases weakens them. It turns meaningful concepts into props. And sure—those lines might impress the naïve, the uncritical, or the overly emotional online crowd. But anyone with a discerning mind, anyone who actually understands leadership or organizational dynamics, can see through it instantly. This wasn’t empowerment. This wasn’t advocacy. This was poor judgment dressed up as a feminist moment. A truly empowered woman knows when to speak—and equally when not to hijack an entire room over a tiny issue that could have been handled privately with her national director. Leaders don’t sabotage the mood of an entire event because they’re triggered by a poorly worded ask. Leaders pick their battles, and they pick their timing. The role of Miss Universe demands diplomacy, composure, and strategic communication. If someone can’t stay calm over a simple promotional request, how will she handle real crises involving politics, culture, or international relations?

text: It’s interesting how this situation mirrors a pattern we see in literature. Characters like Abigail Williams in The Crucible or Becky Sharp in Vanity Fair often start by framing a conflict as a moral crusade — using language of empowerment or victimhood — and for a time, people truly believe them. But as the story unfolds, readers realize that the issue wasn’t oppression or “having their voice silenced,” but rather a case of heightened emotions and poor judgment being packaged as something noble. Once that becomes clear, the public sentiment shifts naturally, not out of malice but out of recognition. In the same way, what initially looked like a dramatic stand for “my voice needs to be heard” or “women’s empowerment” is now being reassessed more calmly. People are starting to see that the conflict may have been less about empowerment and more about emotional mismanagement — which is human, but not heroic.It’s not about tearing anyone down; it’s simply about distinguishing genuine empowerment from moments where emotions get framed as ideology. Literature shows this pattern clearly, and it seems we’re watching a real-life version of it play out. #WhenTheMaskSlips #FromSupportToSideEye #TheShiftIsReal #WeSeeItNow

text: @ItsAndyAntonio  Let's look at the second Q&A, which is the critical question everyone overlooks. The second question wasn’t “give advice to young girls.” It was: “If you win Miss Universe, how will you use this platform to empower girls?” To judge that, you have to ask: Did she directly answer how she would use the Miss Universe platform? Did she give specific, real actions or just metaphors? Was the answer platform-centered, or self-centered? Did she show how the platform would amplify her existing advocacy? When you analyze the answers with that in mind, the contrast is clear: Côte d’Ivoire - Beautiful language, yes. But “being a role model” and “representation” are not platform-based initiatives. They describe who she is, not what she would do. Her answer was elegant, but it did not outline any concrete program, partnership, or action. Pretty isn’t a platform. On the other hand, the Philippines: Ahtisa anchored her answer in substance. She, A) Cited her existing work with an organization helping young people from low-income backgrounds, B) Explained how she would scale and expand that advocacy using the Miss Universe platform, C) Answered the question directly, without fluff or slogans. The Q&A is scored on relevance, clarity, and actionable advocacy, not who delivers the prettiest metaphor. Ahtisa chose impact over embellishment. She didn’t decorate her answer because she didn’t need to. She had a real platform to present. Some viewers prefer a rhetorical flourish. That’s a preference—not a measure of strength in a Q&A round. Now, let's look at the first Q&A question.  The question was “What emotional skill should be taught to children in school?” Côte d’Ivoire answered with “self-love,” which sounds nice but isn’t structurally accurate. Self-love is: emergent, experiential, influenced by family, culture, and environment; it's not something you can teach in a classroom lesson. You can’t guarantee self-love through instruction. It is not a formally teachable emotional skill. Self-awareness would have been the stronger, more correct answer: It is one of the core emotional intelligence skills, it is teachable, and it is foundational to all the others. Meanwhile, Ahtisa’s answers were consistently grounded in accuracy, psychology, and practical application

text:
i think you people worship the wrong things in this reality

-->> worship(n.)
Middle English worshippe, worship, "high respect, honor, fame," from Old English worðscip, wurðscip (Anglian), weorðscipe (West Saxon) "condition of being worthy, dignity, glory, distinction, honor, renown," from weorð "worthy" (see worth) + -scipe (see -ship).

-->> noise(n.)
c. 1200, "sound of a musical instrument;" mid-13c., "loud speech, outcry, clamor, shouting;" c. 1300, "a sound of any kind from any source," especially a loud and disagreeable sound, from Old French noise "din, disturbance, uproar, brawl" (11c., in modern French only in phrase chercher noise "to pick a quarrel"), also "rumor, report, news," a word of uncertain origin, replacing Replaced native gedyn (see din).

According to some, it is from Latin nausea "disgust, annoyance, discomfort," literally "seasickness" (see nausea). According to others, it is from Latin noxia "hurting, injury, damage." OED considers that "the sense of the word is against both suggestions," but nausea could have developed a sense in Vulgar Latin of "unpleasant situation, noise, quarrel" (compare Old Provençal nauza "noise, quarrel"). Confusion with annoy, noisome, and other similar words seems to have occurred.

-->> human(adj.)
mid-15c., humain, humaigne, "human," from Old French humain, umain (adj.) "of or belonging to man" (12c.), from Latin humanus "of man, human," also "humane, philanthropic, kind, gentle, polite; learned, refined, civilized." This is in part from PIE *(dh)ghomon-, literally "earthling, earthly being," as opposed to the gods (from root *dhghem- "earth"), but there is no settled explanation of the sound changes involved. Compare Hebrew adam "man," from adamah "ground." Cognate with Old Lithuanian žmuo (accusative žmuni) "man, male person."

-->> art(n.)
early 13c., "skill as a result of learning or practice," from Old French art (10c.) and directly from Latin artem (nominative ars) "work of art; practical skill; a business, craft," from PIE *ar(ə)-ti- (source also of Sanskrit rtih "manner, mode;" Greek artizein "to prepare"), suffixed form of root *ar- "to fit together." Etymologically it is akin to Latin arma "weapons" (see arm (n.2)).

-->> animal(n.)
early 14c., "any sentient living creature" (including humans), from Latin animale "living being, being which breathes," noun use of neuter of animalis (adj.) "animate, living; of the air," from anima "breath, soul; a current of air" (from PIE root *ane- "to breathe;" for sense development, compare deer).

A rare word in English before c. 1600, and not in KJV (1611). Commonly only of non-human creatures. It drove out the older beast in common usage. Used derisively of brutish humans (in which the "animal," or non-rational, non-spiritual nature is ascendant) from 1580s.

-->> spirit(n.)
mid-13c., "life, the animating or vital principle in man and animals," from Anglo-French spirit, Old French espirit "spirit, soul" (12c., Modern French esprit) and directly from Latin spiritus "a breathing (of respiration, also of the wind), breath;" also "breath of a god," hence "inspiration; breath of life," hence life itself.

The Latin word also could mean "disposition, character; high spirit, vigor, courage; pride, arrogance." It is a derivative of spirare "to breathe," and formerly was said to be perhaps from a PIE *(s)peis- "to blow" (source also of Old Church Slavonic pisto "to play on the flute"). But de Vaan says the Latin verb is "Possibly an onomatopoeic formation imitating the sound of breathing. There are no direct cognates." Compare conspire, expire, inspire.

-->> soul(n.1)
"A substantial entity believed to be that in each person which lives, feels, thinks, and wills" [Century Dictionary], Middle English soule, from Old English sawol "spiritual and emotional part of a person, animate existence; life, living being," from Proto-Germanic *saiwalō (source also of Old Saxon seola, Old Norse sala, Old Frisian sele, Middle Dutch siele, Dutch ziel, Old High German seula, German Seele, Gothic saiwala), a word of uncertain origin.

It has been suspected to have meant originally "coming from or belonging to the sea," the supposed stopping place of the soul before birth or after death [Barnhart]; if so, it would be from Proto-Germanic *saiwaz (see sea). Klein explains this as "from the lake," as a dwelling-place of souls in ancient northern Europe

"The recent controversy around Sabrina Carpenter and White House (U.S. Government / Trump-administration) using her song illustrates some real tensions in music copyright law — so let’s walk through what the law says, what likely applies here, and the gaps / what’s uncertain.

✅ What the law says about using music: rights and licensing

•	Under U.S. copyright law, a song typically involves at least two separate copyrights: (1) the underlying musical composition (lyrics + melody), and (2) the sound recording of a particular performance. Congress.gov+2US EPA+2

•	If someone wants to include a song in a video or advertisement (i.e. combine the music with visual content — audio + video), they generally need two licenses:

1.	A synchronisation (“sync”) license for the musical composition, from the songwriters/publishers. americanbar.org+1

2.	A master-use license for the particular recording, from whoever controls the recording (often a record label). americanbar.org+1
•	If music is simply played at a live event (e.g. rally, concert, in-person gathering), a different license — a public performance license — is needed (unless the venue already has a blanket license). Congress.gov+1

•	For political campaigns or political / government-produced videos (on social media, ads, etc.), these same licensing rules apply: using a song in a video is treated like creating an audiovisual work, so both sync and master-use licenses are required. Congress.gov+1

•	If the user (e.g. politician, government) fails to secure the necessary license(s), that constitutes copyright infringement, and the songwriters/record-owners could bring a lawsuit seeking damages or injunctive relief. Congress.gov+1

•	Also: beyond copyright, there are non-copyright rights that could matter — e.g. a “right of publicity” (using an artist’s name, likeness, or distinctive identity in a way that implies endorsement) or claims under the Lanham Act for “false endorsement”. Those could apply if the video implies that the artist supports or endorses the content. Congress.gov+2Yahoo+2
 
🔎 What this means for the case of Sabrina Carpenter & the White House

Applying this to the recent episode:
•	The White House used Carpenter’s song Juno in a video posted to social media that depicted immigration enforcement/raid footage. The Washington Post+2The Guardian+2

•	Because that was a video (audio + visuals), the White House — legally — should have obtained both a sync license (for the composition) and a master-use license (for the recording). Without both, the use is likely infringing.

•	Carpenter objected publicly, calling the video “evil and disgusting” and demanding the administration stop using her music in that context. The Washington Post+2Sky News+2

•	It appears she and/or her representatives had not granted permission for this use (or at least they say they did not). The Washington Post+2Reuters+2

•	Therefore — provided no license was obtained — the White House’s use of the song likely was a copyright infringement under U.S. law.
Additionally: because the music is being used in a political or governmental context that could be interpreted as endorsing or promoting a particular agenda (immigration enforcement), there might also be right-of-publicity or false-endorsement concerns, especially if the video de facto suggests the artist supports the policies.

So yes — under the standard copyright framework, permission should have been needed, and royalties (or licensing fees) should have been paid to the copyright holders, unless some other legal defence (e.g. fair use) applied."

Let's take, for example, the answers of the top 5 finalists to the final question. Mexico was not the one that gave the best answer. The 5 finalists of the Miss Universe 2025 pageant were asked the same final question during the final Q&A round. Question asked: “If you win the title of Miss Universe tonight, how would you use this platform to empower young girls?” A) Miss Thailand: Delivered general advice to young girls but did not specify how she would use the Miss Universe platform. The statement about “a better world” sounded rehearsed, and her closing line shifted focus toward herself rather than the empowerment of girls. B) Miss Philippines: Directly addressed the question by citing her current involvement with an organization that provides opportunities to young people from low-income backgrounds. She clearly connected her ongoing advocacy to how she would expand it through the Miss Universe platform. C) Miss Venezuela: Spoke about her personal journey of becoming the person she wanted to be. While inspirational, she did not provide examples of helping other girls or explain how she would use the platform to empower them. D) Miss Mexico: Encouraged girls to believe in themselves and use their voices. This remained generic advice and did not answer the specific question about leveraging the Miss Universe platform. E) Miss Côte d’Ivoire: Focused on being a role model and face of representation. While aspirational, her answer was centered on herself rather than on concrete actions she would take using the platform to empower girls. Miss Philippines' answer was strong across all three criteria of Directness, Specificity, and focus, showing clear alignment with the question. Only Miss Philippines explicitly tied her answer to the Miss Universe platform. The other contestants gave broad encouragement rather than actionable strategies. Other answers shifted toward personal identity or self-image rather than the empowerment of girls.
